analysis.one_liner: Forces health plans to fix inaccurate mental health provider directories and meet national network adequacy standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or hearing and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force health insurance plans to fix "ghost networks" — provider directories that list mental health or addiction-treatment providers who are not actually in the network or not taking new patients. Plans would have to verify and update their directories every 30 days, undergo independent annual audits, and publish the results. It would also set national standards for how many in-network mental health providers plans must offer, push plans to pay mental health providers at rates comparable to other medical care, and fund state and tribal ombudsman programs to help consumers with complaints.
analysis.who_benefits: People with job-based or individual insurance who try to use their mental health or substance use disorder benefits would gain the most. The bill targets "ghost networks" — plans whose directories list psychiatrists, therapists, or addiction-treatment providers who are not actually in the network, not accepting new patients, or unreachable — which often force patients to pay out-of-network prices or go without care. It would require plans to verify and update directory information every 30 days, publish audit results, refund patients who were wrongly billed out-of-network rates for providers listed as in-network, fund state and tribal ombudsman programs to help consumers fight denials, and set national standards for how many mental health providers a plan's network must include.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people seeking mental health care

how_it_helps.text: Plans would have to verify their provider directories every 30 days (down from 90) and immediately update entries when a provider stops or starts taking new patients.

Plans would have to commission an independent annual audit of directory accuracy and post the audit publicly, and federal agencies would audit at least 10 plans a year, prioritizing plans with the most ghost-network complaints.

Patients wrongly charged out-of-network prices for providers listed as in-network would be notified in plain language of their right to a refund, and plans would have to regularly reconcile claims against their own directories to catch the errors.

Federal agencies would write the first national quantitative standards for mental health and substance use disorder network adequacy, covering provider-to-patient ratios, appointment wait times, geographic access, and telehealth availability.

Agencies would set a standard for parity in reimbursement rates, so insurers could no longer pay mental health providers far less than medical providers for comparable work — a key reason many clinicians leave insurance networks.
States and tribes could receive $20 million in fiscal 2024 and $10 million a year after that to run ombudsman programs with hotlines that help consumers appeal mental health coverage problems.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans would bear the cost of keeping directories accurate, running independent annual audits, submitting directory data to federal regulators, and paying civil monetary penalties for failures. If regulators set mental health reimbursement rates closer to medical rates, plans' costs for mental health coverage could rise. Providers would also face new duties to report directory changes within days of accepting new patients. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers through premiums.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for insurers and employers — independent annual audits, monthly verification of thousands of directory entries, and federal penalties — would likely be passed on to consumers through premiums.

Providers, including solo practitioners and small practices, would face new legal duties to report directory changes within 5 to 10 business days of accepting new patients, adding administrative work to small mental health practices.

The bill directed agencies to issue major regulations as 'interim final rules' without the usual public notice-and-comment period, limiting the chance for affected parties and the public to weigh in before the rules took effect.

The bill imposed heavy new reporting and rulemaking duties on three federal agencies on fixed timelines, and the appropriations were authorized but not guaranteed, raising questions about whether the audits and ombudsman programs would be funded as written.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targeted is real and well documented: patients seeking mental health care routinely find that directory listings are wrong — the provider is not in-network, is not taking patients, or cannot be reached — leaving them with out-of-network bills or no care at all. The bill's remedies (30-day verification, independent audits, refund reconciliation, national network adequacy and rate-parity standards) attack the problem directly and would cost insurers real money, which is the point. The honest costs are administrative: higher premiums are possible, small providers get new paperwork duties, and fast-tracked rulemaking skips public comment. The design is heavy on new mandates and audits rather than simpler fixes, but on balance it is a consumer-protection bill whose main cost falls on the industry being regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Health Committee from introduction until the Congress ended, and never received a vote of any kind.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the bill on November 15, 2022, joined by Senator Ron Wyden as its only cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no markup, hearing, or vote is recorded in its action history.

The bill would have required plans to verify provider directory information every 30 days instead of every 90, defined 'ghost networks' in federal law, and required independent annual directory audits plus federal audits of at least 10 plans a year.

It would have directed three federal agencies to write national quantitative standards for mental health and substance use disorder network adequacy and a standard for parity in reimbursement rates between mental health care and other medical care.

It also authorized $20 million for fiscal year 2024 and $10 million annually thereafter for state and tribal ombudsman programs, plus $28 million per year from fiscal 2023 through 2032 for the rest of the bill.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill was never taken up again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off: the bill died with no committee vote, so no new directory audits, network adequacy standards, rate-parity rules, or penalties ever took effect. People who struggle to find in-network mental health care gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, free of new audits and standards

sides.party_line_note: Only Democratic senators were attached to the bill — its sponsor and one cosponsor — and no committee or floor vote was ever held, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill imposed directory accuracy duties, independent annual audits, federal audits, civil penalties, and new mental health network adequacy and reimbursement-parity rules on insurers. Each requirement targets a practice — listing phantom providers — that saves plans money by shrinking effective networks.

Employers sponsoring self-insured group plans would have taken on the same directory, audit, and reconciliation duties directly. Many self-insure through insurers that would absorb the work, but the legal duty would sit with them.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Behavioral health providers would have been added to directories more quickly after accepting new patients and would likely see more covered patients as networks became real. They would also carry new duties to report directory changes within 5 to 10 business days.
